title: Java HashMap
learningObjectives: Create a HashMap with key and value types.
Insert and retrieve mappings with put and get.
Check keys and provide default values safely.
Use the Map interface and select HashMap, LinkedHashMap or TreeMap according to lookup and ordering requirements.

understand.concept: HashMap stores key-value mappings and implements Map. Keys are unique; putting a value for an existing key replaces its previous value. HashMap permits one null key and null values, and it does not guarantee iteration order. Use get to retrieve a value, containsKey to distinguish a missing key from a key mapped to null, and getOrDefault for a fallback. Keys should have stable equals and hashCode behaviour while stored.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java hashmap in maintainable applications.
understand.analogy: Think of the collection or date API as a purpose-built tool: its operations communicate the guarantees your program can rely on.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a guide; Java API contracts, equality rules and exception behaviour determine the actual result.

explain.narrative:
Declare both generic types, for example HashMap<String, Integer>. put adds or replaces a mapping; get retrieves by key; remove deletes a mapping. keySet, values and entrySet expose views for iteration. Do not rely on display order. For custom key classes, implement equals and hashCode consistently and avoid mutating fields that participate in hashing while the key is in the map.

## The Map interface and implementations

`Map<K,V>` defines key-to-value mappings. `HashMap` provides hash-based lookup without a guaranteed iteration order. `LinkedHashMap` maintains a predictable encounter order, normally insertion order. `TreeMap` orders entries by key using natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. Declare a variable as `Map<K,V>` when the code needs only the Map contract, then choose the implementation according to ordering and performance requirements.

examples.title: Create mappings
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(); stock.put("Pen", 12); stock.put("Book", 5); System.out.println(stock.get("Pen")); } }
examples.explanation: put stores a value under a key and get retrieves it.

examples.title: Replace an existing key
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>(); scores.put("Asha", 70); scores.put("Asha", 85); System.out.println(scores.get("Asha")); System.out.println(scores.size()); } }
examples.explanation: A map can contain only one mapping for a given key.

examples.title: Use a default value
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<String, String> codes = new HashMap<>(); codes.put("IN", "India"); System.out.println(codes.getOrDefault("US", "Unknown")); } }
examples.explanation: getOrDefault returns a fallback when a key has no mapping.

examples.title: Check before retrieving
examples.code:
import java.util.HashMap;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { HashMap<Integer, String> users = new HashMap<>(); users.put(7, "Mina"); System.out.println(users.containsKey(7)); System.out.println(users.containsKey(9)); } }
examples.explanation: containsKey checks whether a mapping exists.

examples.title: Use Map with LinkedHashMap
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Map<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>(); stock.put("Pen", 4); stock.put("Book", 7); stock.put("Bag", 2); for (String key : stock.keySet()) System.out.println(key); } }
examples.explanation: Map expresses the key-value contract while LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order during iteration. TreeMap is appropriate when entries must be ordered by key.

practise.guidedTask: Declare Map<String,Integer> backed by LinkedHashMap. Insert three products and print entries in insertion order. Then create a TreeMap to show key-sorted order and compare both with HashMap's unspecified iteration order.
practise.independentTask: Build a word counter using Map.merge or getOrDefault. Test a repeated word and an empty input. Explain why Map is an interface and how HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap differ in ordering.
hints: HashMap stores key/value associations and does not guarantee iteration order; use get or containsKey for lookup.
Map.put replaces the value for an existing equal key, so decide whether duplicate IDs should update or be rejected.
Use stable key equality and hashCode implementations, and test missing keys, replacement and null behavior.
practise.challenge: Create a custom immutable key class used in a HashMap. Explain the equals/hashCode contract and why fields participating in hashing should not be mutated while the object is a key.

questions.explanation: Map associates each key with a value.

questions.prompt: Can a HashMap contain duplicate keys?
questions.answer: No; a new value replaces the old mapping
options: No; a new value replaces the old mapping
questions.explanation: Each key identifies at most one mapping.

questions.prompt: Which method checks whether a key exists?
questions.explanation: containsKey checks for a mapping with the given key.

questions.prompt: Which Map implementation orders entries by key?
questions.explanation: TreeMap orders keys by natural ordering or a supplied Comparator.
